column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Seki-gahara, fought on the 21st of October 1600, in central Japan, between the Eastern Army of Toku-gawa Ee-eh-yasu and the Western Army raised in the name of the young heir of Toyo-tomi Hee-deh-yoshi.

Battle of Seki-gahara. On a wet autumn day in 1600, two enormous coalitions fought in the valley of Seki-gahara. By evening, Toku-gawa Ee-eh-yasu was the most powerful man in Japan. The famous story of this battle was written down long afterwards. This introduction separates what the letters of the time say from what later chronicles added. Watch the colour of each tag.

After Hee-deh-yoshi. Toyo-tomi Hee-deh-yoshi had united Japan after a century of civil war. When he died in 1598, his son Hee-deh-yori was five years old. Hee-deh-yoshi left the government to two groups that overlapped: five great lords, the Elders, and five Commissioners who ran the daily business. The strongest of the Elders was Toku-gawa Ee-eh-yasu. Within a year the council was breaking apart. Ee-eh-yasu moved into Osaka Castle and began to act as the ruler of the country.

Two coalitions. In the summer of 1600 Ee-eh-yasu marched north-east against a rival lord, Oo-eh-sugi Kah-geh-katsu. While he was away, his enemies rose in the west. The traditional story makes the Commissioner Ishida Mitsu-nari the leader of the West. Historians today point out that its official commander was the great lord Moh-ree Teru-moto, who stayed in Osaka Castle with the boy Hee-deh-yori. Ishida was its organiser in the field. Many of Hee-deh-yoshi's own generals sided with Ee-eh-yasu. This was not a simple war of loyal men against traitors: Toyo-tomi followers fought on both sides.

The road to Seki-gahara. The West took Foo-shimi Castle near Kyoto after a long siege. Its commander, Toh-ree-ee Moto-tada, died defending it for Ee-eh-yasu. The East took Gifu Castle and advanced on Oh-gaki, where the Western army was gathered. Ee-eh-yasu's son and heir, Hee-deh-tada, led a major Toku-gawa force by the mountain road. Delayed at Oo-eh-da Castle, he did not reach Seki-gahara in time to fight.

The valley. Seki-gahara means "the plain of the barrier". It is a small basin, a few kilometres across, on the Naka-sen-doh, the great road through the mountains between eastern Japan and Kyoto, where roads branch off north and south to Ee-seh. An army that held it held the way to the capital. Around it stand low hills: Mount Sa-sa-oh, Mount Mat-soo-oh, Mount Nan-goo. Whoever held them looked down on the road. The letters written just after the battle do not even call it Seki-gahara: one names the field Ah-oh-no-gahara, another Yamanaka, the village at its western end.

The armies. No reliable, complete count of the men who fought survives. Traditional totals run into the tens of thousands on each side, but many Western troops never joined the fighting. They fought with long spears, bows, swords and matchlock guns, which had come to Japan from Portuguese traders sixty years before. Each lord's men carried his own banners and crests. No one recorded exactly where each army stood. The positions on our map are the traditional camp sites, as marked in the valley today. Historians question some of them.

In the rain, the Western army leaves Oh-gaki and marches west through the dark to Seki-gahara. Why it left is debated: the old story says Ee-eh-yasu lured it out; some historians now think it went to help the Western lord Oh-tani Yoshi-tsugu, whose camp at Yamanaka was in danger.

The day before, Koba-yakawa Hee-deh-aki, a young Western lord with one of the largest Western contingents, takes the hill fort on Mount Mat-soo-oh and turns out its garrison. He has already been talking secretly with Ee-eh-yasu's side.
The Eastern army follows. By dawn its lords stand in the valley, facing the Western camps on the hills, with Ee-eh-yasu on a low hill behind them.

A letter written two days after the battle has been read as placing the start of the fighting at about ten in the morning; later accounts put it earlier. Fukushima Masanori's men attack Oo-kita Hee-deh-ee-eh, the strongest Western lord in the field, while other Eastern lords attack Ishida on Mount Sa-sa-oh.

Some historians read the same letter as saying that Koba-yakawa, and the lords below his hill, turned against the West near the start of the fighting. Others tell the sequence differently. Our reenactment follows the letter. Koba-yakawa's army comes down from Mount Mat-soo-oh and falls on Oh-tani Yoshi-tsugu.

Smaller Western lords camped beside him, among them Wakisaka and Ogawa, change sides as well. Oh-tani's army is destroyed, and Oh-tani dies on the field. Later accounts add that he had foreseen the treachery and held off the first attacks.

On Mount Nan-goo, behind the Eastern army, the great Moh-ree army does not come down. Its vanguard commander, Kick-kawa Hiro-ee-eh, has a secret agreement with the East, and blocks the road. The lords behind him never fight.
With its western flank gone, the Western line falls apart. Konishi, Oo-kita and Ishida flee into the mountains.

Tradition tells it differently. A thick fog fills the valley at dawn. Ee-ee Nao-masa slips past Fukushima's men to fire the first shot. For hours the battle hangs in the balance, while Koba-yakawa watches from his hill. At noon Ee-eh-yasu loses patience and has his guns fire at Mount Mat-soo-oh, and only then does Koba-yakawa come down. On Mount Nan-goo, the Moh-ree messengers are told the army is eating its lunch. These details are best known from accounts written long after the battle; the letters of the time do not mention them.

The Shima-zoo, from the far south of Japan, had stood aside from the fighting. Now, as the Western army collapses, Shima-zoo Yoshi-hiro does not flee west. He leads a desperate breakout through the Eastern lines toward Ee-seh. His rearguard suffers heavy losses, and his nephew Shima-zoo Toyo-hisa is killed protecting the retreat.

By the afternoon the battle is over. Ee-eh-yasu inspects the heads of fallen enemy commanders, as was the custom. Two burial mounds in the valley, the East and West Head Mounds, are remembered as the graves of the dead.

Ishida Mitsu-nari is caught hiding in the mountains. With Konishi Yuki-naga and the monk Ankoku-jee Eh-kay, he is paraded through Kyoto and beheaded, on the first day of the tenth month, the 6th of November in our calendar.

Ee-eh-yasu won a complete victory. No reliable count of the dead survives; estimates run from several thousand to over thirty thousand. Ee-eh-yasu took the lands of about eighty-eight lords who had fought against him, and cut down others. The Moh-ree, whose army never fought, lost most of their domain. In 1603 the Emperor named Ee-eh-yasu show-gun. His family would rule Japan from Eh-doh, the city that became Tokyo, for more than two hundred and sixty years. The Toyo-tomi house survived in Osaka until Ee-eh-yasu destroyed it in 1615. Centuries later, the domains of the Moh-ree and the Shima-zoo, in Choh-shoo and Satsuma, helped overthrow the Toku-gawa shogunate in 1868. That should not be understood simply as revenge for Seki-gahara. Historians still argue about the battle: how long it lasted, when Koba-yakawa turned, and who really led the West. The letters written in its first days are shorter, and stranger, than the famous story.

The famous story of this battle was written down long afterwards. This introduction separates what the letters of the time say from what later chronicles added. Watch the colour of each tag.

After Hee-deh-yoshi. Toyo-tomi Hee-deh-yoshi had united Japan after a century of civil war. When he died in 1598, his son Hee-deh-yori was five years old. Hee-deh-yoshi left the government to two groups that overlapped: five great lords, the Elders, and five Commissioners who ran the daily business. The strongest of the Elders was Toku-gawa Ee-eh-yasu. Within a year the council was breaking apart. Ee-eh-yasu moved into Osaka Castle and began to act as the ruler of the country.

Two coalitions. In the summer of 1600 Ee-eh-yasu marched north-east against a rival lord, Oo-eh-sugi Kah-geh-katsu. While he was away, his enemies rose in the west. The traditional story makes the Commissioner Ishida Mitsu-nari the leader of the West. Historians today point out that its official commander was the great lord Moh-ree Teru-moto, who stayed in Osaka Castle with the boy Hee-deh-yori. Ishida was its organiser in the field. Many of Hee-deh-yoshi's own generals sided with Ee-eh-yasu. This was not a simple war of loyal men against traitors: Toyo-tomi followers fought on both sides.

The road to Seki-gahara. The West took Foo-shimi Castle near Kyoto after a long siege. Its commander, Toh-ree-ee Moto-tada, died defending it for Ee-eh-yasu. The East took Gifu Castle and advanced on Oh-gaki, where the Western army was gathered. Ee-eh-yasu's son and heir, Hee-deh-tada, led a major Toku-gawa force by the mountain road. Delayed at Oo-eh-da Castle, he did not reach Seki-gahara in time to fight.

The valley. Seki-gahara means "the plain of the barrier". It is a small basin, a few kilometres across, on the Naka-sen-doh, the great road through the mountains between eastern Japan and Kyoto, where roads branch off north and south to Ee-seh. An army that held it held the way to the capital. Around it stand low hills: Mount Sa-sa-oh, Mount Mat-soo-oh, Mount Nan-goo. Whoever held them looked down on the road. The letters written just after the battle do not even call it Seki-gahara: one names the field Ah-oh-no-gahara, another Yamanaka, the village at its western end.

The armies. No reliable, complete count of the men who fought survives. Traditional totals run into the tens of thousands on each side, but many Western troops never joined the fighting. They fought with long spears, bows, swords and matchlock guns, which had come to Japan from Portuguese traders sixty years before. Each lord's men carried his own banners and crests. No one recorded exactly where each army stood. The positions on our map are the traditional camp sites, as marked in the valley today. Historians question some of them.

In the rain, the Western army leaves Oh-gaki and marches west through the dark to Seki-gahara. Why it left is debated: the old story says Ee-eh-yasu lured it out; some historians now think it went to help the Western lord Oh-tani Yoshi-tsugu, whose camp at Yamanaka was in danger.

The day before, Koba-yakawa Hee-deh-aki, a young Western lord with one of the largest Western contingents, takes the hill fort on Mount Mat-soo-oh and turns out its garrison. He has already been talking secretly with Ee-eh-yasu's side.
The Eastern army follows. By dawn its lords stand in the valley, facing the Western camps on the hills, with Ee-eh-yasu on a low hill behind them.

A letter written two days after the battle has been read as placing the start of the fighting at about ten in the morning; later accounts put it earlier. Fukushima Masanori's men attack Oo-kita Hee-deh-ee-eh, the strongest Western lord in the field, while other Eastern lords attack Ishida on Mount Sa-sa-oh.

Some historians read the same letter as saying that Koba-yakawa, and the lords below his hill, turned against the West near the start of the fighting. Others tell the sequence differently. Our reenactment follows the letter. Koba-yakawa's army comes down from Mount Mat-soo-oh and falls on Oh-tani Yoshi-tsugu.

Smaller Western lords camped beside him, among them Wakisaka and Ogawa, change sides as well. Oh-tani's army is destroyed, and Oh-tani dies on the field. Later accounts add that he had foreseen the treachery and held off the first attacks.

On Mount Nan-goo, behind the Eastern army, the great Moh-ree army does not come down. Its vanguard commander, Kick-kawa Hiro-ee-eh, has a secret agreement with the East, and blocks the road. The lords behind him never fight.
With its western flank gone, the Western line falls apart. Konishi, Oo-kita and Ishida flee into the mountains.

Tradition tells it differently. A thick fog fills the valley at dawn. Ee-ee Nao-masa slips past Fukushima's men to fire the first shot. For hours the battle hangs in the balance, while Koba-yakawa watches from his hill. At noon Ee-eh-yasu loses patience and has his guns fire at Mount Mat-soo-oh, and only then does Koba-yakawa come down. On Mount Nan-goo, the Moh-ree messengers are told the army is eating its lunch. These details are best known from accounts written long after the battle; the letters of the time do not mention them.

The Shima-zoo, from the far south of Japan, had stood aside from the fighting. Now, as the Western army collapses, Shima-zoo Yoshi-hiro does not flee west. He leads a desperate breakout through the Eastern lines toward Ee-seh. His rearguard suffers heavy losses, and his nephew Shima-zoo Toyo-hisa is killed protecting the retreat.

By the afternoon the battle is over. Ee-eh-yasu inspects the heads of fallen enemy commanders, as was the custom. Two burial mounds in the valley, the East and West Head Mounds, are remembered as the graves of the dead.
